headline: Pemba fishers and government unite to protect ocean, secure livelihoods
meta_description: Over 20 communities in Pemba Island collaborated with Tanzania's government and NGOs to establish two marine protected areas covering 1,300 sq km, reviving fis…
summary_short: Fishers on Pemba Island worked with their government and conservation groups to create two new ocean reserves, turning depleted waters into thriving ecosystems.
body:
On the east coast of Pemba Island, fishermen were returning from the sea with catches that dwindled year after year. Omar Hamad Salim, a fisheries committee member from Tumbe village, watched as his neighbors faced an impossible choice: protect the ocean or feed their families. But this was a false choice. After seeing how an older marine protected area on Pemba's western side had restored fish populations, Salim and more than 20 local communities approached Tanzania's government with a proposal. What followed was a genuine collaboration—communities worked directly with the Department of Blue Economy and Fisheries, along with organizations like the Wildlife Conservation Society and Blue Alliance, to map out two new protected areas covering 1,300 square kilometers of biodiverse waters.

The North-East and South-East conservation areas were officially gazetted in June 2026, protecting coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds that shelter threatened species like reef manta rays. But protection on paper means little without enforcement rooted in community knowledge. Fisheries committees now patrol these waters, monitoring no-take zones and seasonal closures during spawning periods. Salim himself spends his days coordinating committee activities, processing fishing licenses, and enforcing village by-laws against destructive practices like the use of kokoro nets that damage breeding grounds.

What makes Pemba's story remarkable isn't just the scale—it's the model. These are not strict reserves where fishing stops entirely. Instead, communities continue their livelihoods within sustainable boundaries they helped design. As nations race toward the global 30×30 target—protecting 30 percent of land and water by 2030—Pemba demonstrates that meaningful conservation isn't imposed from above. It emerges when fishers, governments, and conservationists listen to each other and trust local leadership.
quick_facts: Over 20 communities collaborated with Tanzania's government on Pemba Island
Two marine protected areas cover 1,300 square kilometers of ocean
Fisheries committees enforce no-take zones and seasonal closures
Areas officially gazetted June 2026, protecting reef manta rays and tuna
